name: Hydrogen
hint: Two hydrogen atoms. One single bond — each H can make only one.
teach: Hydrogen has one electron and needs one more to fill its 1s shell, so it pairs up as H₂.

name: Oxygen
hint: Two oxygens sharing FOUR electrons — promote the bond with a double pinch.
teach: Oxygen needs two electrons, so the atoms share two pairs: a double bond, one σ and one π.

name: Nitrogen
hint: Six shared electrons. Keep pinching to reach a triple bond.
teach: The triple bond in N₂ is 941 kJ/mol — one of the strongest bonds in chemistry.

name: Water
hint: One oxygen, two hydrogens. Oxygen makes two bonds and keeps two lone pairs.
teach: Two lone pairs squeeze the H–O–H angle from 109.5° down to 104.5°, which is why water is bent.

name: Carbon dioxide
hint: Carbon in the middle with a double bond to each oxygen.
teach: Two double bonds = two σ + two π. Linear, so the two C=O dipoles cancel and CO₂ is non-polar.

name: Ammonia
hint: Nitrogen makes three bonds and keeps ONE lone pair on top.
teach: Four electron domains but only three atoms: trigonal PYRAMIDAL, 107°, and a lone pair that makes ammonia a base.

name: Methane
hint: Four hydrogens around one carbon — the perfect tetrahedron.
teach: The textbook sp³ tetrahedron: 109.5°, four identical bonds, completely non-polar.

name: Hydrogen chloride
hint: One hydrogen, one chlorine, one single bond.
teach: ΔEN = 1.0 — a very polar bond. Dissolve it in water and it becomes hydrochloric acid.

name: Beryllium chloride
hint: Beryllium holds only two bonds — the two chlorides push to opposite sides.
teach: Only two electron domains: linear, 180°, sp. Beryllium is happy with just four electrons — a Lewis acid.

name: Boron trifluoride
hint: Three fluorines spread evenly around boron — 120° apart.
teach: Three domains, trigonal planar, sp². Boron has an empty p orbital and only six electrons — hungry for a donor.

name: Hydrogen sulfide
hint: Sulfur sits below oxygen — same shape, wider angle.
teach: Same valence as oxygen, so bent and sp³ — but the angle is only 92° because sulfur barely hybridises.

name: Phosphorus pentachloride
hint: Five chlorines. Period 3 can expand the octet — three equatorial, two axial.
teach: sp³d, trigonal bipyramidal. The axial bonds are longer and weaker than the equatorial ones.

name: Sulfur hexafluoride
hint: Six fluorines around sulfur — the classic octahedron.
teach: sp³d², octahedral, 90°. Twelve electrons around sulfur — and so inert it is used as an electrical insulator.

name: Xenon tetrafluoride
hint: A noble gas! Four fluorines and TWO lone pairs pushed as far apart as possible.
teach: Six domains, two of them lone pairs sitting trans — square planar, sp³d².

name: Ammonium
hint: Ammonia plus one more H — give the nitrogen a +1 charge.
teach: A dative bond: nitrogen donates its lone pair to H⁺. The result is a perfectly tetrahedral +1 ion.

name: Ethane
hint: Two carbons, then fill every carbon with hydrogens.
teach: Every carbon is sp³ and tetrahedral. The C–C bond rotates freely — that is what gives conformations.

name: Ethene
hint: Two carbons joined by a DOUBLE bond — four hydrogens in total.
teach: sp², planar, 120°. The π bond locks the carbons: no rotation, hence cis/trans isomers.

name: Ethyne
hint: A TRIPLE bond between the carbons — only two hydrogens fit.
teach: sp, linear, 180°. Two π bonds and a very short, very strong C≡C — it burns at 3300 °C.

name: Ethanol
hint: Two carbons, then an –OH group on the end carbon.
teach: The hydroxyl makes it polar and hydrogen-bonding — that is why ethanol dissolves in water and ethane does not.

name: Ethanoic acid
hint: A carbonyl (C=O) and an –OH on the same carbon: carboxyl.
teach: The carboxyl carbon is sp² and planar. The –OH proton is acidic because the anion is resonance stabilised.

name: Cyclohexane
hint: Six carbons in a ring — or draw a circle with your finger to build it instantly.
teach: It is NOT flat: the chair conformation keeps every angle at 109.5° and every bond staggered.

name: Benzene
hint: Six carbons in a ring with delocalised π electrons. Open your palm to flatten it.
teach: Six π electrons, Hückel 4n+2 with n = 1: aromatic. Every C–C bond is the same length — 139 pm.

name: Glucose
hint: Six carbons. One is an aldehyde at the end; the other five each carry an –OH.
teach: In solution it closes into a pyranose ring — 99.7% of the time. That ring is what starch and cellulose are built from.

name: Glycine
hint: An amine on one end, a carboxylic acid on the other. Two carbons.
teach: The simplest amino acid. In water it is a zwitterion: NH₃⁺ on one end, COO⁻ on the other.

name: Urea
hint: One carbonyl carbon carrying two –NH₂ groups.
teach: Wöhler made it from ammonium cyanate in 1828 and killed vitalism — organic chemistry needs no life force.

name: Caffeine
hint: A fused purine ring system with three methyl groups and two carbonyls.
teach: A flat, aromatic purine that fits neatly into adenosine receptors — blocking them is exactly how it keeps you awake.

name: Aspirin
hint: Benzene ring with a carboxylic acid and an ester (–OCOCH₃) on adjacent carbons.
teach: Acetylsalicylic acid. The acetyl group permanently blocks COX enzymes — which is why one dose lasts days.

name: Adenine–thymine pair
hint: Build adenine. JARVIS will bring thymine across and form the two hydrogen bonds.
teach: Two hydrogen bonds hold A to T; three hold G to C. That difference is what sets DNA's melting temperature.

name: Hexaamminecobalt(III)
hint: A Co³⁺ centre with six ammonia ligands donating their lone pairs.
teach: Werner proved this octahedron in 1893 and won the first Nobel Prize ever awarded to a coordination chemist.

name: Hexacyanoferrate(III)
hint: An Fe³⁺ centre with six cyanide ligands, each donating through carbon.
teach: The cyanide is bound so tightly that this ion is used as the pigment Prussian blue — and it is not poisonous.
